label: Calling and Purpose
framing: Calling is wider than a career and deeper than a job you happen to like. Scripture roots it first in whose you are before what you do, and it dignifies the ordinary work of hands and home as a place where God is served. You do not have to find one perfect role to live a life that matters.
cultural: In the ancient world a person's work was usually fixed at birth by family and station, and the idea of choosing a path was nearly unknown. Paul told slaves and free, weavers and fishermen, to serve the Lord in the place they stood, which meant the dishwasher and the deacon shared the same dignity, and the work of the hands was never beneath the work of the spirit.
historical: For centuries the church reserved the word calling for priests and monks, until the Reformers of the sixteenth century returned it to the farmer, the mother, and the magistrate, insisting that God is served at the plow as truly as at the altar. The Puritans then taught that a faithful life is built less of grand destiny than of daily duty done well before God.
application: Start not with what is unique about you but with who is in front of you, since calling usually meets you in your obligations before it meets you in your dreams. Do your present work well, as unto God, and let the larger shape clarify over years rather than in a flash. Watch where your gifts and the world's real needs overlap. And measure a life not by its title but by its love.

verses.text: Then the LORD God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
verses.where: Before anything goes wrong in the world, God places the first human in the garden to work it and keep it. Work is part of the good creation, not a punishment.

verses.text: And to Adam He said: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground— because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”
verses.where: After the fall, work remains but becomes toil, with thorns and sweat. The Bible explains why good work can still feel futile and exhausting.

verses.text: And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship,
verses.where: God says he has filled Bezalel, a craftsman called to make the furnishings of the tabernacle, with the Spirit of God. Skill with hands and materials is named as a gift of God's Spirit.

verses.text: Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men, because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving.
verses.where: Paul writes this to slaves in Christian households, people with the least choice over their work. Even there, he says, work done wholeheartedly is service to the Lord, and the Lord will reward it. In the next breath he tells masters to treat their workers justly (Colossians 4:1).

verses.text: Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches.
verses.where: New believers in Corinth wondered whether they had to change their station to follow Christ. Paul tells them that God's call reaches them where they already are, and that they may change their situation if they can, but need not, to serve him.

verses.text: and to aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands, as we instructed you. Then you will behave properly toward outsiders, without being dependent on anyone.
verses.where: Paul urges a young church to aim at a quiet life of ordinary work with their own hands. Steady, unremarkable work is counted as faithful living and a good witness to outsiders.

verses.text: For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.
verses.where: Right after saying that salvation is by grace and not by works, Paul says believers are God's workmanship, made for good works he prepared. Purpose comes after grace, not as a way of earning it.

verses.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
verses.where: Israel asks what offering would satisfy God. The prophet answers with something that fits any job or none: act justly, love mercy, walk humbly with God.

verses.text: Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.
verses.where: After testing pleasure, building and wealth and finding them empty as a way to give life meaning, the Teacher says that to eat, drink and find satisfaction in work is a gift from God's hand. Work cannot be life's meaning, but it can be a gift within it.

verses.text: So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.
verses.where: Paul is settling a dispute about food sacrificed to idols, and widens it to everything: eating, drinking, whatever you do. No part of life is outside the glory of God.

misread.taken: This verse is often given as a personal promise about a career or a dream: God has a plan to prosper you, so the right job or the big break is on its way.
misread.says: Jeremiah wrote it in a letter to the people of Judah taken into exile in Babylon. The “you” is plural, and the promise came with a hard condition: it would be fulfilled after seventy years, so most of the adults who first heard it would die in Babylon. Meanwhile they were told to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the good of the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7). The verse shows God's character: he keeps his promises across generations and has purposes of peace for his people. It does not promise any one reader a better job soon. Its own counsel for exiles is to work faithfully where you are.
misread.text: For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope.

whole: Many people go to work every day and wonder what any of it is for. Some are in jobs that feel meaningless or that grind them down. Some are searching for a calling as if it were a single hidden door, and fear they have missed it. Some have been told, in the church or outside it, that only certain kinds of work really matter, and theirs is not one of them.

The Bible starts in a different place. Work comes before the fall, as part of the good world: God himself works, and he gives the first human a garden to tend. After the fall work becomes toil, which is why even good work can feel futile. But Scripture never splits life into sacred and ordinary. A craftsman is filled with the Spirit, slaves are told their work is done for the Lord, and the call of God reaches people in the situation where it finds them. The deepest calling in Scripture is not first to a job at all. It is to Christ, and then to justice, mercy and humility wherever you are.

So purpose is found more often by faithfulness than by searching. Give yourself to the work in front of you as for the Lord, with care and honesty. Serve the people your work touches. If your situation can change for the better, you may change it; if it cannot yet, it can still be lived before God. Ask what needs you see and what gifts others see in you, and let the church help you discern. And remember the Teacher's warning: work cannot carry the weight of a life's meaning, but received from God's hand, it can be a good part of one.

differ.share: Christians agree that all people are called first to God through Christ, that ordinary work can honor God, and that the church needs the gifts of all its members.

views.name: Every station a calling
views.body: The Reformation tradition, following Martin Luther, teaches that the farmer, the parent and the pastor are equally called by God in their stations, and that daily work is itself a calling.

views.name: Particular callings
views.body: Catholic and Orthodox teaching, and many evangelical churches in their own ways, also speak of particular callings, such as the priesthood, religious life or missionary service, as a special vocation from God, while honoring the work of every believer.

differ.after: Both teach that no honest work is beneath God's notice.

deep.sit: If your work never changed, what would it look like to do it this week as service to the Lord and to the people it touches?

prayer.lead: Psalm 90, the prayer of Moses, ends by asking God to make the work of our hands last.
prayer.text: Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. May the favor of the Lord our God rest upon us; establish for us the work of our hands— yes, establish the work of our hands!
